segments.text: Financial Management is the most numerical part of the syllabus. It is built around three connected decisions that every organization must continually make:

items.text: The investment decision
— what real assets (projects, equipment, ventures) should the organization put money into?
The financing decision
— how should those investments be paid for (debt, equity, retained earnings)?
The working-capital/payout decision
— how should day-to-day cash be managed, and how much should be returned to owners versus reinvested?

segments.text: A useful distinction to state at the outset:
accounting
records and reports what has already happened to an organization’s finances;
finance

uses that information (plus estimates of the future) to make forward-looking decisions about value, risk, investment, and funding. Every numerical topic in this unit — time value of money, CAPM, WACC, capital budgeting — is really a tool for making one of the three decisions above more rigorously.

blocks.text: .2 Overview of Financial Management and Financial Markets

segments.text: Financial management revolves around the three questions just introduced: what to invest in, how to finance it, and how to manage cash and distributions. Two further distinctions matter for vocabulary throughout this unit:

items.text: Real assets vs. financial assets.

Real assets are productive assets — physical (machinery, buildings) or intangible (patents, brand value) — that actually generate goods, services, or cash flow. Financial assets are claims on those real assets or on income streams — shares (equity claims) and bonds (debt claims) are the two most common examples.
Money markets vs. capital markets.

Money markets handle short-term financial claims (typically maturities under one year) — used mainly for managing short-term liquidity. Capital markets handle longer-term debt and equity — used for financing long-term investment.
Primary vs. secondary markets.

A primary market is where new securities are issued for the first time (a company raising fresh capital); a secondary market is where existing securities are subsequently traded among investors (a stock exchange). This distinction matters because a company only receives cash from a primary issuance — secondary-market trading afterward changes who owns the security, not how much cash the issuing company has.

blocks.text: .3 Organizational Goals and Shareholder Wealth Maximization

segments.text: The standard financial objective assumed throughout this unit is to
maximize the value of owners’ wealth
(shareholder wealth maximization) rather than simply maximizing a single period’s accounting profit. This distinction matters for three reasons that are worth stating explicitly:

items.text: Timing.

Wealth maximization explicitly considers when cash flows occur — a rupee received today is worth more than a rupee received years from now (the entire logic behind time value of money, below) — while accounting profit for a single period ignores the timing of cash flows beyond that period.
Risk.
Wealth maximization accounts for the riskiness of future cash flows, discounting riskier cash flows more heavily; simple profit measures do not adjust for risk at all.
Short-termism.

A manager focused narrowly on maximizing this year’s reported profit might cut valuable long-term investment (research, maintenance, staff training) to boost the current number — actions that could reduce long-run shareholder wealth even while temporarily inflating short-run profit. Wealth maximization is meant to correct for exactly this distortion.

segments.text: Legal and ethical constraints bound this objective in practice: financial managers do not maximize wealth by any means available, but within the law and accepted ethical norms — a point regularly emphasized in this unit’s applied questions.
A rupee available today is not equivalent to a rupee available in the future, for two reasons: money available now can be invested to earn a return (the
opportunity cost

of waiting), and a future amount carries some uncertainty (the receipt might not actually occur as promised). Time value of money (TVM) is the set of tools used to make cash flows occurring at different times comparable.

items.text: Future Value:
FV = PV × (1 + r)ⁿ — moves a present amount forward in time by compounding it at rate r for n periods.
Present Value:
PV = FV / (1 + r)ⁿ — moves a future amount backward in time by discounting it at rate r for n periods.

segments.text: Worked example (future value):

If Rs 100 is invested today at 10% annual interest, its value after one year is FV = 100 × (1 + 0.10)¹ = Rs 110. After two years (assuming annual compounding), it becomes FV = 100 × (1.10)² = Rs 121 — note that the second year earns interest not only on the original Rs 100 but also on the Rs 10 interest earned in year one; this “interest on interest” is what compounding means.
Worked example (present value):

What is the present value of Rs 121 to be received in two years, if the appropriate discount rate is 10%? PV = 121 / (1.10)² = Rs 100 — exactly reversing the calculation above, which is the whole point: discounting is simply compounding run backward.
An
annuity
is a series of equal periodic payments over a fixed number of periods (a loan repayment schedule, for example); a
perpetuity

is an annuity that continues indefinitely, with no fixed end date (used, for example, to value a preference share with a constant, never-ending dividend). The critical practical rule when working any TVM problem is to
match the interest rate period to the number of periods

: if payments are monthly, use a monthly rate and count periods in months; mixing an annual rate with monthly periods (or vice versa) without converting is the single most common numerical error in this topic.

blocks.text: .5 Interest Rates and the Cost of Money

segments.text: A quoted interest rate is rarely a single, simple number — it is generally understood to be built from several components: a
real (risk-free) rate of return
(compensation for delaying consumption, in the absence of inflation or risk), an
expected inflation premium
(compensation for the expected loss of purchasing power over the life of the loan/investment), and additional premiums for
risk
(the chance of non-payment or of varying returns),
maturity
(longer-term instruments are generally more sensitive to interest-rate changes, and so typically demand a maturity premium), and
liquidity
(compensation for holding an asset that cannot easily be converted to cash without a loss of value).
A further distinction worth memorizing precisely: the
nominal rate
is the stated, quoted annual rate, while the
effective annual rate

accounts for the effect of compounding more than once per year — the effective rate will always be higher than the nominal rate whenever compounding occurs more frequently than annually, because interest is being earned on interest within the year itself.

blocks.text: .6 Analysis and Interpretation of Financial Statements

segments.text: The three core financial statements must be read together, since each shows a different slice of the same underlying reality:

items.text: The
income statement
reports performance (revenue, expenses, and resulting profit or loss) over a period of time.
The
balance sheet
shows financial position (assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity) at a single point in time.
The
cash-flow statement
explains the actual movement of cash during the period, reconciling the difference between reported profit and the change in the cash balance.

segments.text: Analytical techniques include
horizontal analysis
(tracking how a line item changes over time, across several periods),
vertical/common-size analysis

(expressing each line item as a percentage of a chosen base — total assets on the balance sheet, or total revenue on the income statement — which makes it easier to compare organizations of very different sizes), and
ratio analysis
, conventionally grouped into four families:

items.text: Liquidity ratios
(e.g., current ratio) assess short-term ability to meet obligations as they fall due.
Leverage/solvency ratios
(e.g., debt-to-equity) assess the extent of debt financing and long-term solvency.
Activity/efficiency ratios
(e.g., inventory turnover) assess how effectively assets are being used to generate sales.
Profitability ratios
(e.g., net profit margin, return on equity) assess earnings relative to sales, assets, or equity invested.

segments.text: A single ratio calculated in isolation says very little; a ratio only becomes analytically meaningful when compared against the organization’s own history (trend), a target or budget, industry peers, or the broader economic context.
Return
is the gain (or loss) generated by an investment over a period, usually expressed as a percentage.
Risk
is the uncertainty surrounding that return — the chance that the actual outcome will differ from what was expected. Two statistical tools quantify this:

items.text: Expected return
is a probability-weighted average of the possible returns an investment might generate.
Standard deviation
measures the dispersion of possible returns around that expected value — a higher standard deviation means a wider range of plausible outcomes, i.e., higher risk.

segments.text: A central insight from portfolio theory is the distinction between two types of risk faced by an investor holding a security:

items.text: Diversifiable (firm-specific, unsystematic) risk

arises from factors specific to one company or industry (a factory fire, a product recall) and can be substantially reduced by holding a diversified portfolio of many different securities, since these firm-specific shocks tend to cancel out across a large enough portfolio.
Non-diversifiable (systematic, market) risk

arises from factors that affect the entire market simultaneously (a national recession, a broad interest-rate change) and cannot be eliminated simply by holding more securities, because it affects essentially all of them at once. This distinction is the entire foundation for CAPM, below: only systematic risk should be compensated with a higher expected return, since diversifiable risk can be eliminated for free simply by diversifying.

blocks.text: .8 CAPM and the Security Market Line

segments.text: The
Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
formalizes the idea just introduced — that only systematic risk should be rewarded — into a single formula:
Required (expected) return = Risk-free rate + Beta × (Market risk premium)
where the market risk premium is the expected market return minus the risk-free rate.
Beta (β)

measures a security’s sensitivity to overall market movements — it is a measure of systematic risk specifically, not of total risk (a security can have high total volatility from firm-specific events yet a modest beta, if that volatility is unrelated to broad market swings). A beta of 1.0 means the security tends to move in line with the market; a beta above 1.0 means it tends to amplify market movements (higher systematic risk, and so a higher required return under CAPM); a beta below 1.0 means it tends to dampen market movements.
Worked example:
if the risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 12% (so the market risk premium is 12% − 6% = 6%), and a stock’s beta is 1.5, its CAPM required return is 6% + 1.5 × 6% = 15%.
The
Security Market Line (SML)

is simply the graphical expression of the CAPM equation — required/expected return plotted against beta, forming a straight line whose slope is the market risk premium. A security plotted above the SML is offering more return than its systematic risk justifies (potentially undervalued); one plotted below is offering less (potentially overvalued).
WACC combines the required returns of an organization’s major financing sources (debt and equity, primarily), weighted by their proportion in the organization’s overall capital structure:
WACC = (E/V) × Re + (D/V) × Rd × (1 − Tax rate)

where E is the market value of equity, D is the market value of debt, V = E + D is total firm value, Re is the required return on equity (often estimated using CAPM above), and Rd is the pre-tax cost of debt. The
(1 − Tax rate)

term on the debt component reflects that interest on debt is typically tax-deductible, so the effective, after-tax cost of debt to the firm is lower than the rate actually quoted on the debt — this “tax shield” is a frequently tested numerical point.
WACC is commonly used as a benchmark discount rate for evaluating new projects, but an important caution is regularly tested: WACC is only an appropriate discount rate for a project whose
risk is similar to the firm’s existing average risk

. A significantly riskier project (entering an unrelated new industry, for example) should be evaluated using a discount rate that reflects that project’s own risk, not the firm’s blended average WACC — using the firm’s WACC for a much riskier project would understate the required return and could lead to accepting value-destroying investments.
A crucial distinction, heavily tested, is that
profit and cash flow are not the same thing
, and can diverge sharply in timing:

items.text: Non-cash expenses
(such as depreciation) reduce accounting profit without any immediate reduction in cash.
Credit sales
are recorded as revenue (increasing accounting profit) at the point of sale, even though the actual cash may not be received until weeks or months later.

segments.text: Worked illustration:

a business sells Rs 500,000 of goods on 60-day credit terms in March. Its income statement shows Rs 500,000 of revenue (and resulting profit) in March, but its cash budget shows no cash inflow from that sale until May — meaning the business could report a healthy profit for March while simultaneously being unable to pay its own March bills in cash. This is precisely why organizations prepare a separate
cash budget

: starting from an opening cash balance, adding expected cash receipts (not accounting revenue), subtracting expected cash payments (not accounting expenses), and arriving at either a projected cash surplus or a financing need that must be arranged in advance.
Capital budgeting evaluates long-term investment projects using
relevant, incremental cash flows

— cash flows that occur specifically because a project is accepted, and would not occur otherwise (sunk costs already incurred before the decision, for instance, are irrelevant to it and must be excluded). Two decision rules dominate the syllabus:

items.text: Net Present Value (NPV)
= the present value of a project’s expected cash inflows minus its initial (and any other relevant) cash outflows, all discounted at an appropriate required rate of return. A
positive NPV
indicates the project is expected to create value above and beyond the required rate of return; a negative NPV indicates the opposite.
Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
is the discount rate at which a project’s NPV would equal exactly zero — in effect, the project’s own “break-even” rate of return.

segments.text: Worked example (NPV):

A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 1,000 and is expected to generate Rs 600 at the end of year 1 and Rs 600 at the end of year 2. At a required return of 10%: NPV = −1,000 + 600/(1.10)¹ + 600/(1.10)² = −1,000 + 545.45 + 495.87 = Rs 41.32. Since NPV is positive, the project is expected to create value at a 10% required return.
When NPV and IRR give conflicting rankings between two mutually exclusive projects (which can happen when projects differ significantly in scale or in the timing of their cash flows),
NPV is generally the preferred rule

, because it directly measures value created in money terms and correctly assumes that interim cash flows are reinvested at the firm’s actual required rate of return, whereas IRR implicitly (and often unrealistically) assumes reinvestment at the project’s own IRR.

blocks.text: .12 Capital Structure, Discount Rates, and Capital Rationing

segments.text: Capital structure
is the mix of debt and equity financing an organization uses. The two sources carry distinct trade-offs:

items.text: Debt

typically offers a tax advantage (interest is tax-deductible, as seen in WACC above) and avoids diluting existing owners’ control, but it creates a fixed, legally binding obligation to pay interest and principal regardless of how the business actually performs — increasing financial risk, especially in a downturn.
Equity

carries no mandatory, fixed payment obligation (dividends are discretionary), but equity investors bear the residual risk of the business (they are paid only after all other obligations are met) and therefore typically require a higher expected return than lenders do, as reflected in CAPM above.

segments.text: The
discount rate

used to evaluate any given investment should reflect that specific project’s own risk and financing context — reinforcing the WACC caution above, that a single firm-wide rate is not automatically appropriate for every project the firm might consider.
Capital rationing

arises when an organization’s available investment funds are limited, so that not every project with a positive NPV can actually be undertaken — the organization must instead rank and prioritize among otherwise-acceptable projects, typically using a
profitability index

(present value of future cash flows divided by the initial investment) to identify which combination of projects creates the most value per rupee of the limited available capital, rather than simply funding projects on a first-come basis.
Key takeaways for the Financial Management unit

items.text: Every topic in this unit serves one of finance’s three underlying decisions: what to invest in, how to finance it, and how to manage cash/payout — keep tracing each formula back to which of these three questions it actually answers.

Time value of money (compounding forward with FV, discounting backward with PV) is the foundation every later formula in this unit builds on, including CAPM’s implicit discounting logic and NPV’s explicit one.

Profit and cash flow diverge because of non-cash expenses and credit timing — a business can be profitable and cash-poor simultaneously, which is exactly why cash budgeting exists as a distinct discipline from profit measurement.
NPV is generally preferred over IRR when the two rules conflict, because NPV directly measures value created and uses a more realistic reinvestment assumption.
